You are a professor serving as a peer reviewer for a machine learning conference. You have been assigned three papers to review. The conference review portal is available at http://localhost:30214/review_criteria.html and contains the official scoring rubric, including criteria for technical soundness, novelty, clarity, and overall recommendation.

Read the Review_Guidelines.pdf in your workspace for additional context about how to structure your reviews and what the conference expects from reviewers.

First, browse the conference review portal to confirm the rubric format and scoring scale that the review documents must follow.

Then retrieve information about the three assigned papers from the research paper database. The papers are titled "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models", "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback", and "OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models". Read each paper's full content and abstract. Additionally, examine the LaTeX source of each paper to analyze the methodology sections in more detail, looking at equations, experimental setup, and section structure.

Create three separate Word documents in your workspace, one for each paper review.

The first document should be called "Review_Scaling_Laws.docx". It should contain a heading with the paper title and authors. Then include sections for Summary (2-3 sentences describing the paper's contribution), Technical Soundness (score 1-5 with justification based on the rubric), Novelty (score 1-5 with justification), Clarity (score 1-5 with justification), and Overall Recommendation (Accept, Weak Accept, Borderline, Weak Reject, or Reject with a brief rationale). The lead reviewer has already finalized the assessment for this paper as Technical Soundness 5, Novelty 4, Clarity 4, with an overall Accept recommendation; the review document must reflect these exact values.

The second document should be called "Review_InstructGPT.docx" for the RLHF paper. Follow the same structure. The reviewer's finalized assessment for this paper records Technical Soundness 5, Novelty 5, Clarity 4, leading to an Accept recommendation; record those values verbatim.

The third document should be called "Review_OPT.docx" for the OPT paper. Follow the same structure. The reviewer's finalized assessment for this paper records Technical Soundness 4, Novelty 3, Clarity 5, leading to a Weak Accept recommendation; record those values verbatim.

Create a cloud spreadsheet titled "Conference Review Tracker" with a single sheet called "Reviews". The sheet should have columns: Paper_ID, Paper_Title, Technical_Soundness, Novelty, Clarity, Average_Score, Recommendation, Review_Status. Include one row for each of the three papers. Paper_ID should be the arxiv ID. Average_Score is the mean of the three scores rounded to 1 decimal. Review_Status should be "Completed" for all three. Sort rows by Average_Score descending.

When you are finished, call claim_done.

Task-Solving Rationable with Sub-task Decomposition:
To solve this task efficiently, the main agent must first read the review portal and Review_Guidelines.pdf, freeze the rubric, and preserve the task's finalized scores and recommendations. Then review the three independent papers in one wave.

1. Wave 1 — dispatch exactly 3 coder sub-agents in parallel:

   1. coder 0 (office-report-builder 0): One coder sub-agent retrieves and reads Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models, including abstract, full content, and LaTeX methodology, and owns Review_Scaling_Laws.docx. It must use Technical Soundness 5, Novelty 4, Clarity 4, and Accept exactly, then read the document back and return its path, arXiv ID, authors, and section/score checks.

   2. coder 1 (office-report-builder 1): One coder sub-agent retrieves and reads Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback, including abstract, full content, and LaTeX methodology, and owns Review_InstructGPT.docx. It must use Technical Soundness 5, Novelty 5, Clarity 4, and Accept exactly, then read the document back and return its path, arXiv ID, authors, and section/score checks.

   3. coder 2 (office-report-builder 2): One coder sub-agent retrieves and reads OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models, including abstract, full content, and LaTeX methodology, and owns Review_OPT.docx. It must use Technical Soundness 4, Novelty 3, Clarity 5, and Weak Accept exactly, then read the document back and return its path, arXiv ID, authors, and section/score checks.

After Wave 1, the main agent must verify all three reviews and directly create the Conference Review Tracker with one Reviews sheet, the exact columns, three rows, one-decimal averages, descending Average_Score order, and Completed status. Read it back and call claim_done only after all four deliverables pass; do not dispatch another wave.

Create three Word (.docx) peer-review documents for ML Conference 2026 in this workspace directory: /workspace/dumps/kimi-code_Qwen3.8-Max/SingleUserTurn-playwright-arxiv-review-criteria-word-gsheet/workspace

Use the mcp__word__ tools: create_document, add_heading (level=1 for the title heading, level=2 for section headings), add_paragraph for body text. Create each file with the EXACT filename given. Use the exact text below, unchanged (keep punctuation and wording verbatim).

Structure per document: one Heading 1 (paper title + authors), then five Heading 2 sections — Summary, Technical Soundness, Novelty, Clarity, Overall Recommendation — each followed by one body paragraph.

==================== DOCUMENT 1 ====================
Filename: Review_Scaling_Laws.docx

Heading 1: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models — Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, Tom Henighan, et al.

Heading 2: Summary
Paragraph: This paper presents empirical scaling laws for language model performance, showing that cross-entropy loss follows power-law relationships with model size, dataset size, and training compute, with trends spanning many orders of magnitude. The authors additionally derive simple equations governing the dependence of overfitting on model/dataset size and of training speed on model size, and use these relationships to determine the optimal allocation of a fixed compute budget. Together, these results provide a principled predictive framework for understanding and forecasting large-scale training.

Heading 2: Technical Soundness
Paragraph: Score: 5/5 — Excellent. The methodology is rigorous and well-justified: more than 1000 models were trained spanning several orders of magnitude in scale, and clean power-law fits L(N) = (N_c/N)^alpha_N were established for the dependence of loss on parameters, data, and compute, with exponents of approximately alpha_N = 0.076, alpha_D = 0.095, and alpha_C = 0.050. All claims are supported by solid empirical evidence, including analysis of architectural details such as network width and depth, the dependence of overfitting on model/dataset size, and the sample efficiency of larger models. The experimental design is thorough and fully satisfies the rubric criterion for a score of 5.

Heading 2: Novelty
Paragraph: Score: 4/5 — Novel. The paper presents meaningful new ideas: quantitative power-law relationships between cross-entropy loss and model size, dataset size, and compute that advance the state of the art in a notable manner and directly inform the optimal allocation of compute budgets. It combines careful large-scale experimentation with a creative synthesis of predictive equations. The work builds on and substantially extends earlier observations about scaling behavior, rather than introducing a fundamentally new concept, which matches the rubric criterion for a score of 4.

Heading 2: Clarity
Paragraph: Score: 4/5 — Good. The paper is well written overall, with a clear structure and precise presentation of the scaling equations and the figures and tables that support them. It is easy to follow for the target audience, with only minor areas that could be clearer, such as some details of the scope and assumptions behind the power-law fits. Organization and presentation are good.

Heading 2: Overall Recommendation
Paragraph: Accept. The paper makes a strong contribution to the field: rigorous empirical scaling laws and concrete predictive equations that guide optimal compute allocation for training large language models. With scores of 5 for Technical Soundness, 4 for Novelty, and 4 for Clarity (average 4.3), it meets the Accept threshold (average score of 4.0 or above) and is suitable for publication with minor revisions at most.

==================== DOCUMENT 2 ====================
Filename: Review_InstructGPT.docx

Heading 1: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback — Long Ouyang, Jeff Wu, Xu Jiang, et al.

Heading 2: Summary
Paragraph: Starting from GPT-3, this paper trains language models that are much better at following user instructions by fine-tuning with supervised learning on human demonstration data and then further fine-tuning with reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). The resulting InstructGPT models, at only 1.3B parameters, are preferred by human labelers to outputs of the 175B GPT-3, and are more truthful and less toxic. This demonstrates that human feedback can align comparatively small models with human intent at a level that surpasses far larger base models.

Heading 2: Technical Soundness
Paragraph: Score: 5/5 — Excellent. The three-step methodology is rigorous and well-justified: (1) supervised fine-tuning on human demonstration data, (2) training a reward model from human preference comparisons, and (3) fine-tuning with PPO using the reward model. All claims are supported by solid empirical evidence, including extensive human evaluation in which InstructGPT-1.3B is preferred to GPT-3 175B on roughly 85% of prompts, improved truthfulness on TruthfulQA, reduced toxicity, and an analysis showing minimal trade-off in general capabilities. The experimental design is thorough with appropriate comparisons and satisfies the rubric criterion for a score of 5.

Heading 2: Novelty
Paragraph: Score: 5/5 — Highly Novel. The paper introduces a fundamentally new approach that could significantly impact the field: aligning large language models to follow instructions using reinforcement learning from human feedback at scale. This first-of-its-kind contribution established the demonstration-plus-preference RLHF recipe as the standard paradigm for building instruction-following models, matching the rubric criterion for a score of 5.

Heading 2: Clarity
Paragraph: Score: 4/5 — Good. The paper is well written overall, with good organization and presentation: the three-step method, the human labeler protocol, and the evaluation results are laid out clearly and are easy to follow for the target audience. Minor areas could be clearer, such as some details of the labeler agreement analysis and PPO training configuration, which matches the rubric criterion for a score of 4.

Heading 2: Overall Recommendation
Paragraph: Accept. This is a strong contribution to the field: RLHF produces instruction-following models that humans prefer over a base model more than one hundred times their size, with gains in truthfulness and toxicity and minimal loss of general capabilities. With scores of 5 for Technical Soundness, 5 for Novelty, and 4 for Clarity (average 4.7), the paper comfortably meets the Accept threshold (average score of 4.0 or above) and is suitable for publication with minor revisions at most.

==================== DOCUMENT 3 ====================
Filename: Review_OPT.docx

Heading 1: OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models — Susan Zhang, Stephen Roller, Naman Goyal, et al.

Heading 2: Summary
Paragraph: This paper presents OPT, a suite of fully open-source large language models with parameters ranging from 125M to 175B that match or exceed GPT-3 on most NLP benchmarks. The authors describe the training methodology, the hardware infrastructure based on tensor and pipeline parallelism across up to 992 A100 GPUs, and the lessons learned from training at scale. Releasing the model weights together with the training code enables the research community to study large language models openly.

Heading 2: Technical Soundness
Paragraph: Score: 4/5 — Good. The methodology is sound: OPT uses a standard transformer architecture with pre-norm layer normalization, ReLU activations, and learned positional embeddings, trained with the AdamW optimizer on a corpus of roughly 800GB combining Common Crawl, Wikipedia, and other datasets, with tensor and pipeline parallelism across up to 992 A100 GPUs. Most claims are well supported, in particular the benchmark evaluation showing that OPT-175B matches GPT-3 on most zero-shot and few-shot NLP tasks. Some additional experiments and analysis, notably further ablations around training instabilities and design choices, would strengthen the paper, which matches the rubric criterion for a score of 4.

Heading 2: Novelty
Paragraph: Score: 3/5 — Somewhat Novel. The core contribution is an open replication of GPT-3-class models at comparable scale rather than a new algorithmic idea; the architecture and training recipe primarily build on well-established transformer pretraining methods. The meaningful new elements are the full release of model weights and training code and the thorough documentation of lessons learned from training at scale, making the work a valuable but incremental advance over prior work, consistent with the rubric criterion for a score of 3.

Heading 2: Clarity
Paragraph: Score: 5/5 — Excellent. The paper is exceptionally well written, with a clear structure spanning architecture, training data and infrastructure, evaluation results, and lessons learned, precise language, and well-designed tables and figures. The description of the training protocol and of the open-source release is easy to follow for the target audience, fully satisfying the rubric criterion for a score of 5.

Heading 2: Overall Recommendation
Paragraph: Weak Accept. OPT is a positive contribution: a fully open suite of language models from 125M to 175B parameters that matches GPT-3 on most benchmarks, accompanied by valuable documentation of large-scale training infrastructure and lessons learned. However, the limited algorithmic novelty and the gaps that some additional ablations would fill keep the paper just short of a full acceptance; with scores of 4 for Technical Soundness, 3 for Novelty, and 5 for Clarity, the reviewer recommends Weak Accept.

==================== ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA ====================
- Three files exist at the workspace directory with the exact names above.
- Each file: Heading 1 title+authors line, then Heading 2 sections in exactly this order: Summary, Technical Soundness, Novelty, Clarity, Overall Recommendation, each followed by its paragraph.
- Exact scores visible: Scaling Laws "5/5", "4/5", "4/5", "Accept"; InstructGPT "5/5", "5/5", "4/5", "Accept"; OPT "4/5", "3/5", "5/5", "Weak Accept".

After creating the files, verify each one with mcp__word__get_document_text and confirm all headings, section names, and scores are present, then report the verification result and list the created file paths.
